What You Are Building

An AI Document Intelligence Platform ingests messy PDFs, scans, and images, then turns them into searchable, queryable knowledge. It combines four capabilities: OCR, classification, summarization, and a retrieval-augmented (RAG) chatbot.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of a tireless clerk who reads every document that lands on your desk, files it in the right folder, writes a one-paragraph summary, and then answers your questions by citing the exact page.

Architecture & Components

  • Ingestion + OCR: Tesseract or a cloud OCR API extracts text from scans and images.
  • Classification: a fine-tuned transformer routes each document to a type (invoice, contract, report).
  • Summarization: an LLM produces abstractive summaries per document.
  • RAG chatbot: chunks are embedded into a vector database; a retriever pulls relevant chunks and the LLM answers with citations.
⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Documents are chunked, embedded, and stored. At query time the system embeds the question, does a similarity search, and injects the top chunks into the prompt so the model answers from your data rather than its memory.

Tech Stack & Build Outline

Python, PyTorch or Hugging Face for the classifier, an OCR engine, an embedding model, a vector store (FAISS, Chroma, or pgvector), and FastAPI plus a simple frontend. Build order: (1) OCR pipeline, (2) classifier, (3) summarizer, (4) embed and index, (5) RAG endpoint with citations, (6) evaluation harness measuring retrieval hit-rate.

📝 KEY IDEA

Citations and an evaluation harness are what separate a demo from an engineering project. Show measured retrieval accuracy, not just a chat window.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Skipping chunking strategy. Naive fixed-size chunks split sentences and tank retrieval quality; use semantic or overlapping chunks and test them.

What You Are Building

A Government/UN Knowledge Assistant helps analysts navigate huge, multilingual policy corpora: treaties, resolutions, reports, and legislation. It performs policy analysis and multilingual retrieval so a user asking in one language can find and understand documents written in another.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a research aide fluent in dozens of languages who has read every UN resolution and can answer, in your language, with the exact clause that supports the answer.

Architecture & Components

  • Multilingual embeddings: a cross-lingual model maps text from many languages into one shared vector space.
  • Retrieval layer: a vector store returns relevant passages regardless of source language.
  • Policy analysis module: an LLM compares positions, extracts obligations, and flags contradictions.
  • Answer synthesis: responses cite the source document, language, and article number.
⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Because a cross-lingual embedding model places semantically equivalent sentences near each other across languages, a French query can retrieve the matching Arabic or English clause without machine-translating the entire corpus first.

Tech Stack & Build Outline

Python, a multilingual embedding model, a vector database, an LLM for analysis, and evaluation on multilingual retrieval benchmarks. Build order: (1) collect a public policy corpus, (2) index with multilingual embeddings, (3) build cross-lingual retrieval, (4) add the analysis module, (5) add citations with language metadata, (6) measure retrieval quality across language pairs.

📝 KEY IDEA

Cross-lingual retrieval is the differentiator: matching meaning across languages without translating the whole archive is both cheaper and more accurate.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Relying on a monolingual embedding model and translating everything to English first. This loses nuance and fails on low-resource languages where translation is weak.

What You Are Building

A Quant AI System applies machine learning to markets across three linked tasks: prediction of returns or signals, risk estimation, and portfolio optimization. It turns raw price and fundamental data into disciplined allocation decisions.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of a careful investor who forecasts where prices might go, measures how badly things could swing, and then splits money across assets to get the best expected reward for a tolerable level of danger.

Architecture & Components

  • Data + features: clean time-series, engineer features, and split with a walk-forward scheme.
  • Prediction model: gradient boosting or a sequence model outputs expected returns or signals.
  • Risk module: estimates volatility and covariance to quantify downside.
  • Optimizer: mean-variance or risk-parity allocation converts forecasts and risk into weights.
  • Backtester: simulates the strategy with realistic costs and reports Sharpe and drawdown.
⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Predictions feed expected returns, the risk module supplies the covariance matrix, and the optimizer solves for weights that maximize return per unit of risk, subject to constraints like position limits.

Tech Stack & Build Outline

Python, pandas, scikit-learn or PyTorch, and an optimization library. Build order: (1) data pipeline, (2) features, (3) prediction model with walk-forward validation, (4) risk estimation, (5) optimizer, (6) backtest with transaction costs and metrics.

📝 KEY IDEA

Honest, cost-aware backtesting with walk-forward validation is what makes this credible to quant employers.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Lookahead bias, using future information the model would not have had. It inflates backtest returns and is a red flag to any reviewer.

What You Are Building

An AI Agent Workflow System lets an LLM accomplish multi-step goals by planning, making tool calls, and keeping memory. Instead of one prompt-and-response, the agent decides what to do next, acts on the world, observes results, and repeats until the goal is met.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

It is the difference between an intern who answers one question and an assistant who takes a whole task, breaks it into steps, uses tools like search or a calculator, and remembers what already happened.

Architecture & Components

  • Planner: decomposes a goal into steps and decides the next action.
  • Tool layer: typed functions the agent can call (search, code execution, APIs) with validated inputs.
  • Memory: short-term scratchpad for the current task plus long-term store for facts across sessions.
  • Controller loop: observe, think, act, repeat, with a stopping condition and guardrails.
⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Each iteration the model receives the goal, recent observations, and available tools; it emits an action; the runtime executes it and feeds the result back. This loop continues until the task completes or a limit is hit.

Tech Stack & Build Outline

Python, an LLM with tool-calling, an orchestration framework (or your own loop), and a vector store for long-term memory. Build order: (1) define tools with schemas, (2) build the controller loop, (3) add planning, (4) add memory, (5) add guardrails and logging, (6) evaluate on a task suite with success rate.

📝 KEY IDEA

Observability and guardrails, logging every action and bounding loops, are what make an agent trustworthy rather than a runaway.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Infinite or looping behavior with no stopping condition or step budget, burning cost and producing no result.

The Elite Stack

An elite AI candidate is defined by a coherent stack, not a single skill. It layers up: math (linear algebra, calculus, probability), Python and PyTorch, classical ML, deep learning, LLM engineering, a cloud certification, MLOps, and 5-8 GitHub projects, all reinforced by a research-reading habit.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Employers do not hire a pile of certificates; they hire someone who can take a vague business problem and ship a working, deployed model. The stack is the toolkit that makes that possible.

Target Roles

  • AI Engineer: builds LLM-powered applications and integrations.
  • ML Engineer: trains, deploys, and maintains models in production.
  • LLM Engineer: specializes in prompting, fine-tuning, RAG, and agents.
  • AI Research Engineer: bridges papers and production, running experiments.
  • MLOps Engineer: owns pipelines, deployment, monitoring, and reliability.
  • AI Solutions Architect: designs end-to-end systems for clients.
⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Each role emphasizes a different slice of the same stack. An ML Engineer leans on MLOps and deployment; an LLM Engineer leans on RAG and fine-tuning; a Research Engineer leans on math and paper-reading; a Solutions Architect leans on system design. Your projects signal which slice you own, so tailor two or three flagship builds toward the role you actually want.

How the Layers Connect

The layers are not independent checkboxes; they compound. Math makes deep learning intelligible, deep learning makes LLM engineering more than prompt-guessing, and MLOps plus a cloud certification turn a notebook into a service people can use. The GitHub projects are the visible proof of the invisible foundation, and the research habit keeps the whole stack from going stale.

📝 KEY IDEA

Depth plus proof beats breadth alone. A few deployed, documented projects outperform a long list of unfinished tutorials.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Collecting certificates without shipping anything. Certificates without a portfolio read as tutorial-completion, not engineering ability.

📊 FIGURE — the stack, and why it is a stack
🎯 EXAM TIP
The maths sits beneath deep learning because without it, deep learning becomes trial-and-error tinkering instead of reasoned debugging of architectures and training dynamics. The layers compound: maths makes deep learning intelligible, deep learning makes LLM work more than prompt-guessing, and MLOps turns a notebook into something that serves traffic.

Why Read Research

AI moves fast; the ability to read papers keeps your skills from expiring. Elite candidates build a research-reading habit, following key venues and turning ideas into experiments.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Reading papers is like keeping a doctor's continuing education current: the field changes, and yesterday's best practice becomes tomorrow's baseline.

How to Read a Paper

Use a three-pass approach:

  1. Pass 1: title, abstract, figures, and conclusion, to decide if it is relevant.
  2. Pass 2: read the method and results without getting stuck on proofs, noting the core idea.
  3. Pass 3: reproduce the key equations or code to truly understand it.
⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Most papers do not need pass three. Triage with pass one, extract the idea in pass two, and reserve deep reproduction for the few papers central to your work. This keeps volume sustainable while still building depth where it counts.

Building the Habit

Consistency beats intensity. Reading two or three papers a week, plus skimming a summary newsletter or a few well-chosen threads, keeps you current without drowning. Follow the major venues, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, and ACL, and track a short list of labs and authors whose work matters to your target role. Keep a running notes file where each paper gets three lines: the problem, the core idea, and whether it changes anything you build. Over months this becomes a personal knowledge base you can search, and the act of summarizing forces you to actually understand rather than merely file the PDF away and forget it.

📝 KEY IDEA

Turn reading into doing. A paper you re-implement or apply to a project sticks far better than one you only skim.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Trying to read every paper end-to-end. It is unsustainable and leads to burnout; triage ruthlessly and go deep selectively.

from fastapi import FastAPI, UploadFile
from app import ingest, index, rag

app = FastAPI(title="Doc Intelligence")

@app.post("/upload")
async def upload(file: UploadFile):
    text = ingest.extract(await file.read(), file.filename)
    doc_id = index.add_document(file.filename, text)
    return {"doc_id": doc_id, "chars": len(text)}

@app.post("/ask")
def ask(q: str):
    hits = rag.retrieve(q, k=5)
    return rag.answer(q, hits)   # returns {answer, citations}

Milestone checklist

  1. M0 Setup — repo + docker-compose (api + vector DB) + README skeleton
  2. M1 Ingest & OCR — upload endpoint; extract text from digital + scanned PDFs
  3. M2 Classify — tag each document by type; store metadata
  4. M3 Index — chunk + embed + upsert to the vector store
  5. M4 RAG API — /ask endpoint that retrieves top-k and answers WITH citations
  6. M5 UI — upload + chat interface
  7. M6 Eval & polish — measure retrieval hit-rate + answer faithfulness on a small QA set; write the README with a demo GIF
✅ DEFINITION OF DONE

A user uploads mixed PDFs/scans, asks a question, and gets a correct answer with the source document + page cited. Retrieval hit-rate and a faithfulness spot-check are reported in the README. One-command startup (docker-compose up).

⚠️ PITFALLS TO AVOID

Skipping OCR quality checks (garbage in → garbage out); no citations (looks like a toy); over-large chunks that dilute retrieval; leaking PII from sample docs into git; trusting the LLM without grounding. Always ground answers in retrieved text and show sources.

Stretch goals (to stand out)

  • Table & form extraction (Azure Document Intelligence layout)
  • Multilingual documents
  • Hybrid search (BM25 + vectors) with reranking
  • Per-user access control on documents
📊 FIGURE — overlapping chunks, and where code lives
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Counting chunks with overlap

The first chunk covers tokens 1–500. Because each subsequent chunk repeats 50 tokens of the previous one, it only advances the window by 500 − 50 = 450 new tokens.

chunks = 1 + ⌈(5000 − 500)/450⌉ = 1 + ⌈10⌉ = 11

Sanity-check the ends: chunk 11 starts at token 1 + 10(450) = 4501 and runs to 5000, so it is the last one needed and nothing is left over.

The common wrong answer is 10 — from dividing 5000/500 and forgetting that overlap makes the chunks advance more slowly than their size.

🎯 EXAM TIP
With overlap, chunks advance by size − overlap, not by size: 5,000 tokens at 500/50 gives 11 chunks, not 10. And in the playbook's layout, app/rag.py is the module holding retrieval, grounded prompt construction and the cited answer — ingest.py does upload and OCR, index.py chunks and embeds, schemas.py defines the request/response models.

def answer(query, hits, threshold=0.35):
    if not hits or hits[0].score < threshold:
        return {"answer": "I could not find this in the provided documents.",
                "citations": []}
    context = "\n\n".join(f"[{h.doc}#{h.section}] {h.text}" for h in hits)
    prompt = (SYSTEM_GROUNDED + "\nContext:\n" + context +
              f"\n\nQuestion: {query}\nAnswer ONLY from the context and cite [doc#section].")
    return llm(prompt)  # -> {answer, citations}

  2. M1 Ingest — parse policy PDFs; retain section/article metadata + language
  3. M2 Multilingual index — embed + upsert; verify a query in language A finds docs in language B
  4. M3 Retrieve + rerank — top-k then cross-encoder rerank
  5. M4 Grounded answers — cite article/section; refuse when nothing relevant is retrieved
  6. M5 Guardrails — injection defense, scope check, low-confidence flagging
  7. M6 Eval — faithfulness + retrieval recall on a bilingual QA set; document limitations honestly

⚠️ PITFALLS TO AVOID

  • Human-in-the-loop review for flagged answers

⚠️ PITFALLS TO AVOID

Lookahead bias (using future data in features/scaling) — the #1 quant mistake. Also: overfitting to one backtest, survivorship bias, ignoring transaction costs/slippage, and p-hacking parameters. If results look too good, you almost certainly leaked data.

  • Risk parity allocation
  • Bayesian/uncertainty-aware predictions
  • Live paper-trading with a broker API
📊 FIGURE — scaling by the square root of time
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Working the annualisation

The daily Sharpe ratio is the mean daily return divided by the daily volatility:

0.0004 / 0.008 = 0.05

Returns accumulate linearly with time while volatility grows with √time, so the ratio scales by the square root of the number of periods:

0.05 × √252 = 0.05 × 15.8745 ≈ 0.79

Multiplying by 252 instead would give 12.6 — an implausible number that should itself be the warning sign, since real strategies rarely exceed a Sharpe of about 2.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Annualise a Sharpe ratio by multiplying by √252 ≈ 15.87, not by 252: 0.04%/0.8% daily gives 0.05, and 0.05 × 15.87 ≈ 0.79. The square root appears because returns scale with time while volatility scales with its square root.

def run(goal, tools, max_steps=8):
    messages = [{"role":"system","content":SYSTEM},

Sizing & Serving Any ML System

Every design answer follows the same spine: requirements to numbers to architecture to metrics to failure modes. Clarify scale (QPS, DAU, item count), the latency SLA, and the business objective before drawing a single box.

FRAMEWORK
  • Funnel: candidate generation (recall, cheap, millions to thousands) then ranking (precision, expensive, thousands to tens) then re-rank/policy (business rules, diversity, guardrails).
  • Two-tower retrieval for candidate gen; an ANN index (HNSW/IVF) for sublinear lookup; heavy cross-features only in the ranker.
  • Feature store = one transform, two readers: batch (training) and low-latency (serving) from the same definitions to kill skew.
HOW TO REASON

Estimate top-down: QPS = DAU x actions/user / 86,400, then peak = 2-5x average. Storage = rows x bytes. Embeddings = N_items x dim x 4 bytes. If the ranker is P50=15ms and you need P99<100ms, cap candidates so tail x model-cost fits the budget, and cache hot results.

CHECKLIST
  1. Objective plus guardrail metric (engagement up, but complaint rate must not rise).
  2. Online vs batch: if it needs freshness or personalization to the last click, go online; else precompute.
  3. Log features at serving time to guarantee train/serve parity.
  4. Shadow, then canary, then A/B with a pre-registered primary metric and MDE-driven sample size.
  5. Fallbacks: cache, default ranker, degrade gracefully on dependency loss.
RED FLAG

Training on features unavailable at inference (label leakage / future data); point-in-time joins prevent it. Also: optimizing an offline proxy (AUC) that never moves the online metric, and making A/B decisions on a metric peeked before significance.

📊 FIGURE — recommending with no history
🎯 EXAM TIP
The standard mitigation is to use content/metadata features in a hybrid model and add exploration to gather feedback. Both halves matter: content features give a zero-history item a representation immediately, and exploration collects the interaction data collaborative filtering needs — without it the item never accumulates the history that would let it be recommended.

Diagnosing and Trusting a Result

Applied rigor means ruling out the boring explanation before the interesting one: leakage, skew, and bad metrics masquerade as both breakthroughs and failures.

FRAMEWORK
  • Gap reading: train low + val high = overfit / too little regularization or data; train high + val high = underfit or bug; train ~0 + val perfect = leakage.
  • Metric to problem: imbalanced = PR-AUC / recall@precision; ranking = NDCG/MAP; threshold decisions need calibration = Brier/ECE; regression tails = quantile loss.
  • Adapt ladder: prompt, then RAG, then fine-tune; move down only when the cheaper rung provably fails the need.
HOW TO REASON

Suspicious win? Check the split (grouped/time-based?), search features for the label or a proxy of it, and confirm the test set was never touched during tuning. A loss spike then divergence points to LR too high; a plateau far above zero points to capacity, features, or a data bug.

CHECKLIST
  1. Split by entity/time to avoid leakage across near-duplicates.
  2. Establish a baseline (majority class, simple model) before celebrating.
  3. Choose the metric from the decision it drives, not from convention.
  4. Report variance across seeds/folds, not a single run.
  5. Inspect errors by slice; aggregate metrics hide subgroup failure.
RED FLAG

99.9% accuracy on a rare-event task (just predicting the majority). Random splits on time-series or grouped data. Tuning on the test set. Fine-tuning to inject knowledge that changes hourly (that is a retrieval problem). Comparing models at different operating thresholds.

📊 FIGURE — two diagnoses from the shape of a curve
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two signatures worth recognising instantly. Training loss falling while validation loss bottoms out and then rises is overfitting past the optimum — apply early stopping, regularisation, or more data. And a deployed model decaying gradually with unchanged code is data or concept drift — monitor feature and prediction distributions, and retrain on recent representative data.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.

23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
